title: Lay out a meal by the clock face for a crewmate who cannot see
instruction: Lay out the meal for the crewmate seated at the left end, who cannot see. By the clock face as they sit, put the blue cup at 2, the green pouch at 7 and the orange spoon case at 11 o'clock, 10 cm from the plate centre.
context: The clock-face method tells a person who is blind or has low vision where food and drink sit: 12 o'clock is the far side of the plate from them and 6 o'clock the side nearest them. Carers and hospital staff use it, including for patients whose eyes are patched. Eye injuries from foreign bodies are among the most common medical events on the station, and a lunar base would see the same. On Earth this is assistive-robot work in homes and care facilities, done in 1 g at a table, as here. The test is applying a named convention centred on another person's body: the diner sits at the end of the table, so their clock is turned 90 degrees from the arms' view. Taking 12 as straight ahead of the arms, or reading the clock for someone facing the arms, puts every item at a wrong hour and scores 0, and so does a conventional place setting laid for the arms' own seat.
setup: Station table, in front of the left arm; the right arm is idle at its ready pose. Table coordinates in metres: x forward from the line through the two arm bases, y left from the midline, heights above the table top; the left arm's base is at (0, 0.305). Every part is a rigid matte primitive with one friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic). Fixed, the diner stand-in at the left (+y) end of the table, facing -y along it: a slate blue (sRGB 0.30, 0.35, 0.50) torso block 300 mm along x, 120 mm along y and 160 mm tall, centred at (0.240, 0.580), square behind the plate, so it spans x 0.090 to 0.390 and y 0.520 to 0.640; and a beige (sRGB 0.82, 0.70, 0.58) head, an upright cylinder 100 mm across and 100 mm tall, centred on the torso's top face. Fixed, a white (sRGB 0.95, 0.95, 0.95) plate, a disc 120 mm across and 12 mm tall, centred at (0.240, 0.320), its centre 200 mm from the torso's front face. On the diner's clock 12 o'clock points -y (away from the diner, toward the right of the top camera image), 3 o'clock -x (the diner's right, toward the arms), 6 o'clock +y and 9 o'clock +x. Loose, standing on the table in a supply row at y = 0.150, long axes along x: an orange (sRGB 0.95, 0.55, 0.10) spoon case, a block 70 mm along x, 28 mm along y and 30 mm tall, 35 g, at x = 0.140; a green (sRGB 0.30, 0.65, 0.30) food pouch, a block 60 mm along x, 40 mm along y and 25 mm tall, 60 g, at x = 0.220; and a blue (sRGB 0.20, 0.45, 0.85) cup, a solid cylinder 40 mm across and 70 mm tall, 60 g, at x = 0.300. The items are 80 mm apart centre to centre, 171 to 197 mm from the plate centre, outside the scoring band, and each at least 60 degrees off its own hour. The demo's targets: the cup at 2 o'clock, 100 mm out, at (0.153, 0.270); the pouch at 7 o'clock, 100 mm out, at (0.290, 0.407), its 60 mm side along the radius; the spoon case at 11 o'clock, 110 mm out, at (0.295, 0.225), its long axis along the radius so its inner end stays 15 mm off the rim. Every start and target lies within 0.34 m of the left arm's base, and every centre at least 110 mm from the torso. To build it: a box 300 x 120 x 160 mm with a 100 mm tube glued on top, painted slate blue and beige, stands in for the diner (use the stand-in, never a person, at the robot's table); a 120 mm white disc 12 mm thick for the plate; a 40 mm printed or wooden cylinder weighted to 60 g for the cup; printed or wooden blocks weighted to 60 g and 35 g for the pouch and the case. Tape the plate and the stand-in down and mark the three start spots.
scoring: End state only, judged after the arm has released and moved clear, from a top photo, a tape measure and a protractor centred on the plate; in simulation on the final step. Bearings run clockwise seen from above, from the diner's 12 o'clock (-y, the far side of the plate from the diner), 30 degrees per hour: the cup's 2 o'clock is 60 degrees, the pouch's 7 is 210 and the spoon case's 11 is 330. An item counts when all of these hold: it is at rest (under 10 mm/s and 0.5 rad/s); it is level, the cup standing on either end with its axis within 8 degrees of vertical, the pouch and the case lying or standing on any face within 8 degrees of level (a case leaning on the plate rim tilts 9.9 degrees); its lowest point is within 3 mm of the table top, so not on the plate, on another item or still held at the 5 mm release height; its centre is 85 to 125 mm from the plate centre (the instruction's 10 cm, -15 to +25 mm, as the plate rim limits the inner side); and the bearing of its centre is within 15 degrees of its hour. Score = counted items / 3, so 0, 1/3, 2/3 or 1.0. Success, which ends the trial, is all three counted, held for 1 s. The items may be carried, slid or turned any way; only the end state counts. The start state scores 0: every item is 171 to 197 mm from the plate centre and at least 60 degrees off its own hour. Sliding the whole row straight toward the plate and the diner, or pulling each item straight in toward the plate, also scores 0; a straight slide of the row brings at most one item to its hour, and only when aimed at it. Hours are 30 degrees apart, so one 15 degree band never covers two hours, and an item at another item's hour earns nothing. Reference outcomes: taking 12 as straight ahead of the arms (+x) puts the cup at the diner's 11, the pouch at 4 and the case at 8, 0. Reading the clock for someone across the table, facing the arms, puts them at 5, 10 and 2, 0; for someone at the other end, 8, 1 and 5, 0. Running the diner's clock counterclockwise puts them at 10, 5 and 1, 0. A conventional setting laid for the arms' own seat (cup at its upper right, pouch to its left, spoon case to its right) puts them at 10:30, 6 and 12, 0. A conventional setting for the diner with the cup at 2, the case to their right at 3 and the pouch to their left at 9 earns only the cup, 1/3. Values exactly on a limit pass (0.1 mm margin). In simulation every test uses each item's centre and quaternion, not its axis-aligned bounds, and the scorer reads object poses, not the gripper, so an item held still with its bottom within 3 mm of the table would count; on the real rig the photo after the arm withdraws decides. The plate and the stand-in are fixed in simulation; on the real rig a trial in which the plate moves more than 5 mm from its mark scores 0.
reset_notes: Nothing is consumed. Stand the cup, the pouch and the spoon case back on their marks in the supply row, long axes along x; the plate and the diner stand-in do not move. Run with -E object_jitter=0: the layout and the open-loop demo depend on it.
fidelity: Approximate: blindness is only the story, as the scene has no sensory model, and the diner is a fixed block with a cylinder head. The cup, pouch and spoon case are solid rigid primitives with one shared friction (1.2 static, 1.0 dynamic) and matte colours; no food, liquid or utensils. The plate is a 120 mm disc, about half the size of a dinner plate, so the layout is at about half scale. Earth gravity on a table, which is where meals are set out.
